items.prose: The clock in this app ticks every 100 µs. A Monte Carlo pricer takes about 50 µs per call.
items.question: How many calls must one timed batch hold for the tick to be at most 1% of the batch time?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. First find how long the batch must last.

byKey.two: Two calls last 100 µs, one tick: the error can be 100%.
byKey.hundred: You divided 10,000 by the tick. Divide by the time per call, 50 µs.

explain.text: One tick is 1% of $100 / 0.01 = 10{,}000$ µs, and $10{,}000 / 50 = 200$ calls. Time the batch, then divide by 200.

items.question: What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The results are unused, so the optimiser removed the calls
The 100 µs tick rounds a long run down to 0
options.why: A million calls take tens of milliseconds, hundreds of ticks. The tick cannot hide that.

options.text: C++ really prices a million calls in under a microsecond
options.why: Each call evaluates `log`, `exp` and two `erfc`s: tens of nanoseconds at least, so tens of milliseconds in all.

options.text: The first call was a warm-up and was not counted
options.why: Nothing here skips any calls; `time_us` times the whole lambda.

feedback.correct: Keep the results alive: add them to a sink you print.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What happens to each call's result?

explain.text: `bs_call` has no side effects, so unused results let the optimiser delete the whole loop. Write `sum += bs_call(...)` and print `sum` after timing.

items.question: About how long does it take at $n = 600$, in µs?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The tree does about $n^2/2$ updates.

byKey.lin: You doubled the time. The work grows as $n^2$, so doubling $n$ multiplies it by 4.

items.prose: A flat lattice for $n = 100$ stores node $(i, j)$ at `v[i * (n + 1) + j]`.
items.question: At which index is node $(10, 4)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each row holds $n + 1 = 101$ places.

byKey.n: You used rows of 100. A row holds $n + 1 = 101$ nodes.

explain.text: Row 10 starts at $10 \times 101 = 1{,}010$, and node $j = 4$ is four places further: 1,014.

items.question: What is the fastest correct change?

options.text: Swap the two loops, keeping the index `i * cols + j`

options.why: `reserve` only sets aside room for future `push_back`s. It does not change the order the loops read memory.
Rows in separate blocks do not help a column walk, and the copy costs more than the sum.
On the desk run, `-O3` left the column walk about 7 times slower than row by row. The access pattern is the problem.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which loop order reads memory in order?

explain.text: With `i` outside and `j` inside, the inner loop reads consecutive doubles, eight per cache line. The sum is the same; the walk is several times faster.

items.question: What does a build with `-DNDEBUG` print?

options.why: That is the debug build. With `NDEBUG` the whole assert, `++trades` included, is removed.

options.text: Nothing: the assert fails and stops the program
options.why: Under `NDEBUG` the assert is not evaluated at all, so it cannot fail.
`assert` with `NDEBUG` expands to an empty statement, which compiles.

feedback.correct: The side effect vanished with the assert.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `assert(x)` become under `NDEBUG`?

explain.text: With `NDEBUG`, `assert(++trades == 1)` expands to nothing, so `trades` stays 0. Do the work outside: `++trades; assert(trades == 1);`.

items.prose: After adding `-ffast-math`, the desk's nightly P&L total moves in the 12th significant figure and a NaN check on input volatilities stops firing.
items.question: What should the desk do?

options.text: Remove `-ffast-math`: it reorders sums and lets the compiler assume NaN never appears
Keep it and loosen every test's tolerance
options.why: Loosening tolerances hides real bugs too, and it does not bring back the deleted NaN check.
That is slow and still breaks IEEE rules. The flag is the cause.

options.text: Nothing: the 12th digit does not matter
options.why: The missing NaN check matters: bad inputs now get priced.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which flag changed both behaviours?

explain.text: `-ffast-math` allows reassociation and assumes no NaN or infinity, so sums change and `std::isnan` can be folded to `false`. Use `-O2` without it.

items.prose: You must test a new `bs_put`. `bs_call` is already trusted.
items.question: Which test can catch a wrong `norm_cdf(d2)` inside `bs_put`?

options.text: Parity: `bs_call - bs_put` against `S - K e^{-rT}` within 1e-9
Compare `bs_put` with the put formula written out again in the test
options.why: If the test copies the formula, it copies the mistake, and both sides agree.
The wrong put is 16.92, positive too. The check cannot fail on this bug.
The correct put is 5.57352602..., so `==` fails on the right answer as well.

feedback.correct: Parity uses the trusted call as an independent reference.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which test does not reuse the code under test?

explain.text: Parity holds in any arbitrage-free model, and `bs_call` is trusted, so a wrong put breaks it. The wrong put gives 16.92, far from 5.57.

items.prose: At $n = 512$ the correct tree is 0.004 from Black-Scholes. A tree that stops at 64 steps is 0.031 away.
items.question: Which tolerance should the convergence test use?

options.why: That passes the tree stuck at 64 steps, 0.031 away, so the test cannot catch that bug.
The correct tree is 0.004 away, so this fails the right answer.
A tree never equals Black-Scholes exactly at finite $n$.

feedback.correct: Above the true error, below the bug's error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The tolerance must sit between 0.004 and 0.031.

explain.text: A tolerance must pass the known error, 0.004, and fail plausible bugs, 0.031. 0.01 sits between with room on both sides.
